maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make some remarks concerning a matter which I deem to be of great importance. I had intended to discuss this matter when the Estimates of the Labour Department were considered in committee, but as I do not know when those Estimates will come before us, and as there is a campaign, being carried on in the press in the meantime, I think it my duty to present the facts with respect to this question now, and offer such comments as I consider necessary. I will first state the facts of the case as I know them to be, and then repeat the version of them as given in the press.
On March 23, a delegation of the Executive Officers of the National Labour

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS

speechtext:
The Minister of Labour, on Wednesday, received a deputation representing the National Catholic Labour movement in this province, whose members asked, among other things, that the organization be represented at the forthcoming conference of building trades representatives, to be held in Ottawa, The Catholic Federated Unions in Quebec, apcording to Abbd Fortin, a member of the deputation, has a membership of from forty to fifty thousand, and is therefore an important factor in the industrial life of this province. The Minister of Labour, the Hon. Gideon Robertson, appears to have adopted a very extraordinary attitude in dealing with this deputation. He seized the occasion to lecture the Union in regard to its religious complexion, saying that an impression that success in labour in Quebec was conditional upon holding a certain religious belief would not be conducive to Improved relations between Quebec and other provinces. Then he proceeded to say that the coming conference was organized by the international unions and the builders, and that he could not dictate to either party for the purpose of admitting a third.
The Minister of Labour has, on a number of occasions, acted as if he were the Minister of Organized Labour; he now comes forward as the Minister of Organized Labour Internationally Affiliated. When provision was first made for the establishment of a Department of Labour in connection with the administration at Ottawa, such a situation as this was never contemplated; the idea and purpose was to create a department which would keep in touch with all classes of labour and would deal equally with all. Certainly it was never supposed that a Minister of Labour, in dealing with a labour body, would concern himself with the religious convictions of its members. The Catholic National Union in this province is none the less a labour organization because its membership is Catholic, nor is it the business of the Minister of Labour to dwell upon, or even consider, the religious belief of this labour body or of any other, Catholic or Protestant. The impression created, however, is that the minister's real objection to the Quebec unions is that they are national. Mr. Ernest Lapointe, who introduced the deputation, and Abbd Fortin, who headed it, seem to have been under no illusion in this respect. It was not the first time that these national unions had asked in vain for representation. The reasons for refusal vary, but the refusals do not. Moreover, the minister indicates clearly enough what is in his mind, and what his purpose is. when he emphasizes the fact that the building conference has been organized by builders and members of international unions. Is he not really concerned for the supremacy of the international organization? He says that all nations subscribing to the peace treaty have agreed to recognize associations giving each class (employers and labour) the greatest representation, and the labour organization in Canada, which conforms to this standard, is the Trades and Labour Congress. Here is internationalism again. , There is nothing in the labour provisions of the peace treaty which authorizes more favourable treatment to one class of

labour than to another; the whole spirit of the treaty is to the contrary, and if Canada, as a subscriber, has agreed to deal only with the Trades and Labour Congress, it is the first intimation that we have had of it. The people of Canada have never sanctioned any such injustice and will nbt do so. As to the building trade conference, it is being held under government auspices, if it is not actually government financed, and if the Minister of Labour desired to secure representation for the Catholic unions, nobody will believe that his efforts would be unsuccessful.
In the Montreal Gazette of Thursday, March 31, appears a letter signed by G. D. Robertson, Minister of Labour. This letter is very long, but I think in all fairness I should read it in its entirety. I am sure that the House will bear with me while I do so. It is as follows:
.	National Catholic Unions
To the Editor of The Gazette:
Sir,-In your issue of March 24, 1921, and editorial appeared entitled "Showing His Hand" which charges the Minister of Labour with being the "Minister of Organized Labour Internationally Affiliated," which charge you base upon his statement to the National Catholic Union that he could not undertake to force the Federal Builders' Association and -the Federal Building Trades Council who are holding a conference in Ottawa on May 3rd next, to recognize National Catholic Union delegates.
Your implied support to the impossible position taken by Mr. E. Lapointe (Quebec East) indicates utter ignorance of the facts, or else an endorsation of the National Catholic Union principles and policies. It is, therefore, proposed to relate some facts concerning International Trade Unions; the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and what it represents; the National Catholic Unions, and the policy and attitude of the Department of Labour toward each.
For forty years past craft organizations of workmen, with members in both the United States and Canada, have existed. They are known as International Trade Unions. Every person engaged in a particular trade or craft is eligible for membership, subject to certain requirements as to moral character, sobriety, etc. Catholic and Protestant alike enjoy equal rights and privileges. The constitutions provide that neither religious nor political affiliations shall affect in any way a workman's eligibility to membership. Many of the constitutions specifically forbid the discussion of religious or political questions within the union. Briefly stated, every workman has and should have equal rights and voice in the industri-al field. Neither religious nor political affiliations should be a recommendation or a bar to obtaining employment.
To these principles the Minister of Labour heartily subscribes. Mr. Lapointe does not; does the Montreal Gazette?
The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada is and has for years, both by past and present Governements, been the recognized legislative mouthpiece of labour in Canada. It does not-as your paper has frequently asserted-represent Trades Unions only ; neither does it speak for all the International Unions, a number of whom maintain their own legislative representatives. There are over 70.000 railway employees in Ca-

nada members of International Trade Unions who are not represented through the congress, including the organization of which the undersigned has for twenty-five years been a member. Therefore your oft-repeated inference, i.e., that the Minister of Labour was guided by the wishes of the Trade Congress, is obviously not a fact nor a near approach thereto.
The Trades Congress does, however, speak for many labour bodies that are not International in character, but purely local and purely Canadian, as the following facts will verify. At the Hamilton convention of the Congress, held in September, 1920, the 929 delegates present represented about 280,000 workers-232 came from the province of Quebec-five of these delegates represented five International Unions- nine represented four trade councils-218 represented 101 local unions in that province. These delegates represented 88,949 organized workers in that province, a large portion of which are Roman Catholics. The senior vice-president of the Congress is a Roman Catholic, resident in Montreal. Like the International Unions the Congress stands for equality among all workers, so far as their rights and privileges within their respective organizations are concerned, and also in their opportunities for employment regardless of religious or political affiliation of the individual. Both the International Unions and the Trades Congress are in accord with the prin ciples laid down in the pastoral letter circulatec in September, 1918 by the archbishops and bishops of the United States, signed by the late respected and lamented Cardinal Gibbons of Baltimore, Md. Except in Quebec, throughout all North America, Catholics and Protestants alike, other citizens as well as workmen, endorse the principles giving equal right to all, and everywhere-except in Quebec-millions of workmen, representing every shade of religious opinion, are able to work together in harmony.
To the universal application of these principles the present Minister of Labor subscribes. Mr. Lapointe does not-does the Montreal Gazette?
The National Catholic Union movement began at the city of Three Rivers in 1911, extending to Chicoutimi in 1912 and 1913. The published report on the subject, dated 1913, reads in part as follows:
"The object of the organization is the protection and development of the religious, social and economic interests of its members. The association is essentially Catholic and professes its belief in and entire submission to the instruction and direction of that Church. The qualifications for membership require a candidate to observe -the Catholic faith, to be of not less than 16 years of age, and not connected with an International Union. There are both active and honorary members. The affairs are administered by an executive committee chosen by the council of direction. There is to be a general chaplain named by the Ordinary of the diocese. Each local branch also has a chaplain named by the Ordinary of the district. The constitution provides for small death and permanent incapacity benefits provided the member's marriage was legally contracted under the rites of the Catholic Church."
There were at that time nine branches, with a membership of 1,567. At that date there were in the province of Quebec 37,928 organized workmen adhering to the principle of absolute equality referred to in a preceding paragraph.
By 1919 troubles had occurred in certain localities, because of discrimination against

Protestants and Catholic workmen members of other trade unions. An attempt was made to minimize this difficulty by passing the following resolution, at at Three Rivers convention of September, 1919 :
"(Resolution 19) Whereas certain rumors have circulated that the National Catholic Unions do not protect Protestant workmen in labor matters, this convention allows the adoption of a resolution protesting against such a statement and energetically states that it has protected and is still protecting Protestant workmen in all labor matters by issuing to them an adjunct membership card which guarantees to them all the protection they need."
Investigation shows that this adjunct membership card permitted the holder to pay dues but debarred him from any voting power in the Union.
Perusal of the constitutions reveals some interesting facts. That of the Catholic Union of the Quebec Printing and Book Binding Workers may be of interest to the Montreal Gazette. It reads in part as follows:-
"Chapter 1, Article 1:-
'"There is founded in the city of Quebec between the Catholic workers following the printing and book binding trades, an organization which shall be designated as follows: The Catholic Union of the Quebec Printing and Book Binding Workers.	'
"Art. 2. The Union has for its immediate object the study, protection and development of the professional interests of its members; but it subordinates this proximate object to the exigencies of the superior interests of souls, society and religion.
"Art. 3. Because it is a Catholic labour organization, the Catholic Union of the Quebec Printing and Book Binding Workers ;
"(a) Shall affiliate with the Action Sociale Catholique;
"It shall secure from it, after filling the usual conditions and upon presentation of its statutes and by-laws, a special diploma which shall be the warranty of the Catholicism of the Union ;
"iSaid diploma may be cancelled or revoked in' case the' Union should cease to fulfil the conditions required for its affiliation ;
''(b) It , shall admit among its members Catholic workers only ;
"(c) It shall have a Chaplain;
"(d) It shall remember,
"1.-That all human acts, those of groups as well as those of individuals, are subjected to the tribunal of conscience ;
"2.-That justice and Christian charity are the two.su/preme mannitory rules or relations between employers and workmen;
(e). Recognizing that the Church alone has the right and is qualified to say where, in the so-called labour questions, is the true and the false, the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, what is permissible and what is not, the C.U. of P. and B.W. will comply entirely and conscientiously, in the pursuit of its object, wtith the teaching and instructions of the religious authority.
"(f). In order to still shows its character as a Catholic Union the C.U. of P. and B.W.
"(a) Puts itself under the protection of St. Joseph.
"(b) It shall cause to be celebrated every year, on the Feast Day of its Holy Patron Saint, a solemn mass with a sermon, all members endeavouring to attend and receive Holy Communion.
''(c) When a member dies the Union shall cause to be celebrated in the Church where the
funeral takes place a high mass for the repose of the Brother's soul and shall be represented at said mass by at least two of its members.
"Chapter II.-Membership, admission and exclusion.
"Art. 4. The Catholic Union of Printing and Book Binding Workers of Quebec is composed of an unlimited number of members ;
"Art. 5. To become a member of the C.U. of P. and B.W. one must:
"1.-Be an active Catholic.
"2.-Be at least 18 years old; follow (as linotype machine operator, case worker, pressman, feeder, binder, finisher and ruler) the printing or book binding trade since at least five years, or that of stereotyper since at least three years and hold a certificate of competency (as journeyman) delivered by the Union itself.
"All those who, being 16 years old have followed the printing or book binding trade for at least two years, may also be members of the Union, but as apprentices and without having any right to vote at meetings, if they otherwise fulfil the other conditions of admission.
"3.-Belong to no secret society or any organization the principles, tendencies and spirit of which do not agree with those of the union.
''Chapter III.-Executive Committee, Council, General Assembly.
"Art. 8. The- Union is directed and administered by an Executive Committee, a Council, and a General Assembly of members.
"Art. 9. The executive committee is composed of the President, Vice-President-or in his absence the Assistant Secretary and the Treasurer of the Union, elected in February of each year and re-eligible at the expiration of their term of office, by the General Assembly of members of the Union, and the Chaplain of the Union, appointed by His Grace the Archbishop of Quebec.
"11. The Executive Committee is directed to administer the property of the Union, to dispatch daily and routine business, and to carry out the decision of the General Assembly, to the direction of which it remains subject and to which it gives an account of its operations and conduct. It is its duty to call regular meetings, or, if need be, special meetings of the Council and General Assembly and to settle itself all matters relating to such calls.
"III.-The Executive Committee, meets once a week at the place, date and hour fixed by itself. As to special meetings of the General Assembly the President of the Union shall call them if four members of the Union request him in writing to do so.
"Art. 19. The Council is composed of the members of the Executive Committee and three Councillors elected in February of each year, and re-eligible at the expiration of their term of office by the General Assembly of members.
"The Council has all the powers necessary for the direction of the management of the affairs of the Union in particular:
"It admits, refuses, or excludes members, after consulting the General Assembly.
''It settles all matters in connection with the enforcement of the by-laws of the Union and the putting into practice of the principles which the Union recognizes as governing its action.
"Art 12. The Chaplain is appointed by His Grace the Archbishop of Quebec. He is a member of the Executive Committee, Council, and General Assembly. He takes part in all debates but does not vote. He may, however, require that any resolution be submitted to the Archbishop of Quebec and approved by him before taking effect, and any resolution adopted dur-

ing his absence must be communicated to him before being carried1 out."
The apprenticeship by-laws provide that:
'T. The selection of apprentices belongs to the employer, and no one shall be allowed, without his consent, to work in printing and book binding shops ;
"2. All apprentices shall be at least 14 years of age and must have shown a sufficient knowledge of the French language to the satisfaction of both the employer and the union."
The foregoing clearly shows that the purpose is Church control of an organization of industrial workers. Note that no resolution can pass or be adopted without the chaplain's consent, who will in turn-if he is in doubt-submit same to the bishop, whose decision is final, regardless of the wishes of the membership. Note too that apprenticeship is required, and that the applicant must have the endorsation of the union as to his ability to speak French. No Protestant, and no Catholic connected with any other organization of workmen is eligible for membership. Why? Obviously because they cannot be satisfactorily controlled by the Church authorities.
May I relate just two instances of how the application of the National Catholic Union principles work out. During 1919 the Department of Labour received a complaint that it was difficult, if not impossible, for any but National Ca/tholic Union members to get employment in the Davies shipyards at Lauzon. It was also observed that the dry dock operated by that company was built with public money and protested vigorously against Protestant or Catholics, not members of the National Catholic Union, being debarred from employment. On February 23rd, 1920, a French-Canadian Catholic filed complaint that two painters, members of the International Painters' Union, working on the Drill Hall at Quebec City, were dismissed by the contractors because they would not join the National Catholic Union. The complaint stated this was the second instance of discrimination against them. Briefly stated, the conflict arises because of the determination of Church authorities to autocratically control industry and industrial workers, discriminating against those who do not bow to their dictation.
To such a policy the present Minister of Labour will never subscribe ; Mr. Lapointe does ; does The Montreal Gazette?
Finally, your paper supports Mr. Lapointe in his endorsation of the National Catholic Union request for representation at the conference of the National Industrial Council of building employers and workmen. I wonder why?
The Dominion Association of Building Contractors and the trade unions representing the building trades in Canada, did, in 1919, lay the foundation for active co-operation between employer and employee in that important industry. They have established local industrial councils in several large cities with a central or appeal court to which local disputes unadjusted may be referred. On the Central Council each interest has equal representation, but no chairman. Both interests asked the Department of Labour for its co-operation in providing an official of the department to act as convenor of and preside at the central council meetings, but without any voting power, his advice on questions under consideration being solicited by both. The development of the Co-

operative Industrial Council idea is growing and the object of the conference on May 3rd is to encourage it among those who have found it possible to work together in harmony. The delegates are being invited upon the nomination of the employers' and workmen's respective organizations. The National Catholic Union delegates would be gladly invited if the consent of the parties participating were obtained, but instead of approaching them the National Catholic Union make a demand on the Labour Department to force representation for them, which request was declined. Why did the National Catholic Union make this request instead of seeking to co-operate with the two parties in* terested? One reason is because in January 1919, it issued a statement from Quebec, which reads in part as follows:
"The National Central Trades Council of the District of Quebec assumes it its duty, under the present circumstances, to make the following statements:
"1. This Council represents in Quebec the national and Catholic labour movement. It voluntarily assumes responsibility for its own decisions and measures, but it has nothing to do with other labour groups whose principles, claims and programmes are not entirely its own.
"The National Central Trades Council of the District of Quebec is, moreover, absolutely a stranger to all the doings of the Uabour party' of the Province of Quebec, and has no relation whatever with either the 'Trades and Labour Congress of Canada' or the Trades and Labour Council of Montreal.
"The National Central Trades Council of the District of Quebec is autonomous, of a national spirit, distinctly Catholic."
. Having voluntarily cut themselves off from intercourse with all other labour bodies, knowing the impossibility of securing any recognition or co-operation from them, the National Catholic Union now demands that the Department of Labour force their unwelcome presence upon this conference, the only possible effect of which would be to destroy its usefulness. They knew the department could not lend itself to such a proposal, therefore a good opportunity presented itself for Mr. Lapointe to endorse a project calculated to provoke discord and, at the same time, blame the Government for it, and you lent the support of your paper to the trick.
I hope you will give this letter the same publicity as your editorial received.

Minister of Labour.
Ottawa, March 27, 1921.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
and what was the occasion for the attack upon the catholicity of the National Catholic Unions? That attack was made and has been repeated by the Minister of Labour as minister, and the Government should either repudiate it or take the responsibility for it.
When this letter and that article appeared in the Gazette, I referred to the 'natter in the House, and as I wish to quote exactly the facts of the matter, I quote here what I then said:

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Before you proceed with this item, Sir, the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said last night that he intended to proceed with the Estimates of the Labour Department to-day. The Estimates of that department have not been taken up previously, and I will object to their being proceeded with to-day. Before we proceed with the Estimates of the Labour Department, I have a few remarks to make about the hon. gentleman who I presides over that department and about certain matters concerning it.
Then there was a meeting of the trades council in Ottawa, at which Mr. Moore, the president of the Trades and Labour Congress, and Mr. P. M. Draper, of that association, delivered speeches. The report of this meeting appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of April 2, 1921. I shall quote only a few words of what Mr. Moore said:
Attempted Supercession
"As long as the leaders of that movement confined their operations to their own province, we were not interested," said Tom Moore, "hut ' we find that the National Catholic Union seeks to supersede the International Trades Union at the Dominion Industrial Conference. It attempted to do this a year ago, and is again renewing the attempt. To the everlasting credit of the Hon. Senator Gideon Robertson, Minister of Labour, he has held that religion shall not be mixed up with the labour movement. Because of this Mr. Lapointe, the member for Kamouraska, has announced his intention of taking the Minister of Labour to task on the floor of Parliament, and has said that he will challenge the Estimates of the Labour Department, in order to hold up the appropriation for the industrial conference, and force the Government' to recede from the stand it has taken on this question."
Mr. P. M. Draper spoke as follows:
"Politicians have been guilty in the past of dividing our people on religious grounds in order to attain the seats of the mighty, but we don't want any of this kind of thing in our movement. We must send good men speaking both languages through Quebec to show them the issue underlying this dangerous movement, and I think when they understand they will tell their clergy, "You had better confine your attentions to our spiritual affairs, and leave us to look after our own business.' "
At that meeting a resolution was passed, a copy of which was sent to the members of the districts surrounding the city of Ottawa. I shall read one of its clauses:

Whereas this Trades Council, appreciating the danger to the International Trade Union movement and the organized workers of this country, should the Minister of Labour be overruled in his correct attitude to the non-recognition of any factional or religious movement in coming Building Trades Conference or any other Government committee or commission-
Therefore this Council declares its full commendation of the position taken by the Minister of Labour, etc.
In justice to the National Labour Unions, I desire to read a very short interview given by one of its officers, which appeared in all the Canadian newspapers yesterday. It was dispatched by the Canadian Associated Press and reads in part:
Quebec, April 3.-The National Catholic Unions have known for a long time the sentiments of the Minister of Labour towards them, but they wished to ascertain the reasons for his attitude, said Abbe M. Fortin, general almoner of the unions, in an interview to-day. "The minister made known the reasons for his attitude at the Interview we recently had with him in Ottawa and in his letter published in the press," added the abbe.
"The Minister of Labour continues to mix into matters that do not concern him," he continued. "Instead of giving a serious answer to the demands made by us at Ottawa he persists in entering into a discussion of a question, which as minister of the crown he should leave alone.
"We did not go to Ottawa to ask the minister's approbation for our unions and we do not see the necessity of knowing whether or not the principles of the National Catholic Unions please him or not. As Minister of Labour he has only to enquire whether or not our unions menace the public interest. He has, however, carefully avoided putting such a question as, during the past five years, the National Catholic Unions have been the ones which have contributed most to the maintenance of public order."
Refering to Senator Robertson's contention in his letter to the press that the church through the priests attached to the unions controlled the deliberations and policies of the unions Abbe Fortin said that the function of the almoners was to prevent the workers in the course of their deliberations, from breaking the doctrines of the church. "The Catholic workers like the others," he added, "deliberate freely and make whatever decisions seem good to them. The function of the almoners is that of councillors and not controllers."
My comments, Mr. Speaker, shall be few. I am not a member either of the National or of the International Labour Union. I am a friend of labour, especially of organized labour, and have endeavoured in my public career to acquaint myself with the various labour problems and the claims of labour, and the remarks I intend to make shall be imbued with a spirit of goodwill for the cause and the interests of labour. The argument I desire to offer I shall try to base entirely upon principles of justice and fairness, upon principles which must appeal to all men irrespective of their

creeds, their opinions, and their personal differences, and even to those belonging to either of the two labour bodies which are the cause of the present difficulty. We have in Canada a Department of Labour that was created by legislation of this Parliament about fifteen years ago. (My hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) informs me that it is twenty years ago.) The duties and the work of the Department of Labour are prescribed by various statutes of this country. The department must work in such a manner as will ensure peace in the field of industrial activity. In various statutes relating to the department is a reference to unions and trade unions, and I may refer especially to the Industrial Disputes Act, which provides that when either the employer or a labour or trades union appeals to the minister regarding labour difficulties, a board of arbitration shall be appointed to settle the question at issue. The Minister of Labour is entrusted with the high and important duty of assisting in the maintenance of industrial peace in this country, and he must see that there is harmony as between employers and employees as well as among employees themselves. The very nature of his functions obliges him to be fair and impartial in his dealings with all sections of labour. If,-owing to lack of vision, narrowness of mind, bias, or otherwise,-he cannot be fair and impartial, his usefulness is gone and he is only a cause of trouble and discontent. When reference is made, in the statutes that I have just quoted, to "Labour Union" it is never said that it must be an International Union. It is not specified what sort of a union it has to be in order to get recognition from the Government or the Department of Labour. In none of these statutes can you see any proviso that such union has to be affiliated with the Trades and Labour Congress, or whether it has to recognize the jurisdiction of the American Federation of Labour. I do not wish to express any preference as regards the International Union to which the Minister of Labour belongs, or the National Unions which he has fulminated against. Both organizations have a valuable and most important work to perform, both have a large field of activity, both have the right to existence and recognition; and I shall not fall into the mistake which has been committed by the Minister of Labour of assailing or abusing either of these two labour bodies. I shall willingly go as far as to admit that personally
the Minister of Labour is quite entitled to prefer the International Union to the other; but I say tfcat in his public capacity, acting as the head of the Department of Labour, he has no right to discriminate against either union and to refuse to give it, in all his dealings with labour, proper and effective recognition, proportionate to its membership. Freedom of association is not a privilege which any Minister of Labour can destroy. Trade unionism is a natural and normal development in the field of industry. The working man when left alone, struggling single handed and individually, was in a painful state of inferiority in dealings with the industrial owner. He Was frequently forced, on account of his weakness, to accept unfair conditions and unjust terms. Trades unionism has raised the standard of labour. Its aims are to realize for the working man a higher scale. It attempts to improve not only the material but also the moral, social and spiritual conditions of the members who compose it. It works not merely for the sake of mere life, it exists for the sake of good life. It is, indeed, a sort of mutual insurance body working for the betterment of the social and moral as well as the material conditions of the working man.
. Now, Sir, in the realization of that ideal there are people who believe that religion has an important part to play. Others think that religion should be wholly ignored by, and excluded from, all that concerns labour associations. Some people believe that religion is a force in determining sociological work; that it is religious spirit which, more than anything else, teaches a man that his service must not only be for himself but for humanity-that he must view problems and difficulties in more than material aspects. They believe that religion and sociology are co-forces working in harmony both determining the destiny of man, and surely it is not a crime to believe in such association. Others believe that all labour unions should be absolutely neutral and purely business associations, and that they will achieve their end more successfully by remaining so; and they have the right to believe so, their opinion is entitled to respect. But, Sir, neither the advocates of the first nor those of the second system have the right to force their view upon the others, nor to impose their preference upon those who honestly differ from them in this most important problem. Even the Department of Labour, under its present head, has preached a doctrine different from that expounded now by the minister.

I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued by the Department of Labour entitled "Information Respecting the Russian Soviet System and its Propaganda in North America" in which it is said, on page 18:
The National Catholic Unions are located in the Province of Quebec and are very antisocialist.
It is not that phrase I want to refer to, but another one on the same page which reads as follows:
Trade Unions which retain within their ranks men who use their membership to "bore from within," and destroy instead of support, are assuming a serious responsibility and risk. There is unquestionably need of an opportunity for work by the Christian Churches of every denomination.
So the Minister of Labour himself was inviting the co-operation of the Church. I do not desire to say a word as to the merits or demrits of the existing unions. I merely claim that so long as they exist side by side, so long as they are lawful organizations working for industrial peace in the land, they are both entitled to recognition from the Government, and the Minister of Labour has no right to side officially with one against the other, and to attack and grossly misrepresent either, as he has done in the case which I am now discussing. Our constitution guarantees equally to each citizen the protection of the law. Sir, the trade unions have had to fight for a great many years, and in some instances are still fighting, for existence and recognition. Why should the old ones try to kill the new ones? They are both tending towards the same goal, but believe in different agencies and methods of action.
The Canadian doctrine is, equality of rights under the law. When a man appeals for his rights he appeals to the principle of right, and what he appeals to for himself he must recognize as equally good in regard to others. Hence he is under a moral obligation to recognize the rights of others. The man who asks for "my" rights does not ask for them because they are his rights exclusively. When a man asks for his rights and gets them, and then because he is stronger than another man refuses to him the rights which he has claimed for himself, it is not right but might that is triumphant.
On February 21 and 22, 1921, a conference of employers and employees was held in Ottawa, and a report of that conference has been published by the Department of Labour under the title: Report of the Conference on Industrial Relations. In that report I find this passage in a speech de-

livered by the Minister of Labour, which I would commend to him if he were a member of this House. It will be found on page 58 of that report:
1 do not think any employer in this country questions a man's right to be a member of any fraternal soceity or church, and I think there are very few who even ask an employee whether he is a member of a trades union or not; but I think there is a tendency on the part of some employers to refrain from dealing with their workmen through their unions.
And he pleads with the employer for the recognition of those unions. How can the Minister of Labour reconcile that appeal with his own attitude with regard to the National Labour Union? I believe in selfdetermination in labour organization as in any other fields of activity. Workingmen have a right to honestly differ as to the character, the programme, and the activities of the associations which they clesire to form or join.
I have referred to the religious element of the question, but there are other points of difference. I have here the platform of the Trades and Labour Congress as published in the Ninth Annual Report of the labour organizations for the calendar year 1919. In that platform there are many planks which, of course, every one is entitled to support. I wish to refer especially to a few of them. The first is free compulsory education; the second is the legal working days of six hours, and six days to a week; the third is government inspection of all industries ; and so on. The eighth is abolition of the Dominion Senate. Well, it is a piece of humour that the Minister of Labour should be a member of the Senate-when one of the planks of the Trades and Labour Congress is the abolition of the Senate. Article 15 of the platform calls for direct legislation through the initiative and referendum. And so on. But there is more than that. I see in the same report of the Department of Labour that prior to 1902 there were national unions in the province of Quebec which were affiliated with the Trades and Labour Congress, but they were expelled from the congress. Here is what the report says on page 42:
As has been reported in previous departmental annual reviews of labour organizations in Canada, the majority of the independent labour units in the Dominion were to be found in the province of Quebec, and principally in the city of the same name. Some of the older national unions of Quebec were at one time affiliated with the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, but by an amendment to the constitution in 1902, the congress denied recognition to national unions where international organizations of the same craft existed. This decision also deprived the

national unions from representation on trades councils chartered by the congress.
I see on page 131 that this article still exists in the constitution of the congress. Part of section 2 reads as follows:
Further, no national union or local unions comprising said national unions shall he entitled to membership in this congress when there is in existence an international union of their craft, nor shall any local union attached to a national body separated from their international organization, or any organization which has been expelled or rejected by the American Federation of Labour, be entitled to delegates in any central body chartered by this congress.
So, Mr. Speaker, apart altogether from the religious point of view, and purely from the national standpoint, all working men who do not believe in some of the planks of the Trades and Labour Congress, or indeed a subordination of their unions to the American Federation of Labour-and surely they are entitled to their opinion in that respect-have no alternative but to join an independent union, and the Minister of Labour and the Government have no right to interfere with the exercise of their discretion in the matter. On the other hand, those workingmen who believe that the larger organization is safer and more powerful for the protection of their rights and interests are entitled to their opinion also, and no Government or department of labour should interfere with them.
Now, Sir, the Minister of Labour has set forth the argument that he was governed by a clause of the labour agreement and the Peace Treaty concerning the International Labour Conference, to which each party to the League of Nations would send four representatives, and that two of those representatives would be appointed by each government, the two other representatives being appointed one to represent labour and the other to represent employers. He states there is a disposition that provides that the choice of the representatives of labour and of employers will be made by the organizations, when such exist in the country, which are most representative of the workingmen or of the employers. Well, that is no argument at all. At the International Labour Conference the representation of labour and of the employers was limited to one delegate each. I agree that it was the fairest method of choosing delegates at that conference to let the most powerful labour organization, or the one whose members were more numerous, choose the delegate for Labour, and to let the most representative of employers' organizations choose the representative of the employers. But is that a
reason to deny recognition to the other labour unions at conferences where labour is represented by ten, twenty, or fifty delegates? Is that a reason to give to one labour union full control of the representation of labour at all conferences?
I have here the Labour Gazette of November, 1920, a publication issued by the Labour Department, in which there is an article with regard to the Industrial Council in Belgium, exactly the same kind of body as that which is going to sit in Ottawa in the month of May next. On page 1508 of this issue of the Labour Gazette,
I find the following with reference to the Council of Mines, a most important industrial council of Belgium:
The workers' representatives are appointed by the two industrial unions in proportion to their membership, the socialist union having eight and the Christian Roman Catholic union having two.
It is not only in Belgium that such unions are recognized. They are recognized in Ireland; they are recognized in Italy. No department of labour in any other country thinks of interfering with or denying existence or recognition to a particular branch of trade unionism. What is the purpose of a joint industrial council? I have here another report of the Department of Labour on the Industrial Councils, on page 31 of which I find what I consider to be the best definition of the duties of a joint industrial council. It is as follows:
First, to secure the largest possible measure of joint action between employers and work people for the development of the industry as a part of national life and for the improvement of the conditions of all engaged In that industry.
To make a joint industrial council successful it must represent as far as possible all the parties interested in that particular trade; there must be a fair representation of .all the interests concerned if their decrees are to command willing and general assent. Each section has its own interests, slightly or greatly diverging from the interests of the other section. If consultation, joint conferences-indeed, self-government in industry-are to grow, it will be necessary that all separate interests have their fair share of representation, and it should be the business of Parliament to see that they get it.
Now, I think every member of the House will agree that any man of impartial mind presiding over the Department of Labour, any man qualified to fill that important office, instead of trying to crush and abuse any of the labour bodies of Canada, should

try to use some tact and diplomacy with the view of getting: them together to cause them to co-operate with each other instead of being divided against each other. And when, Mr. Speaker, the officers of one of the unions which are excluded from government conferences or commissions go to the Minister of Labour and say:	We are
ready to co-operate with you and with the other labour bodies in Canada; we want to attend the conference; if our numbers entitle us to only one or two or three delegates, give us one or two or three that is all, we want to work with our brethern in the other labour associations-when they say that, the Minister of Labour should not tell them:	The others refuse to go with
you; the others will refuse to sit with you at any conference. But the minister did say that, and he approved of that attitude. I repeat that it should be the duty of the Minister of Labour to get these unions together, not to divide them, because it is only through co-operation at these conferences that all may get together and work for industrial peace and harmony in this country.
With regard to the statement of Mr. Moore that I said in the House that I wanted to prevent the adoption of the Estimates, of the Department of Labour, the Estimates to cover the expenses of the coming conference, in saying that, he deceived his hearers at that time, as the House well knows. I never said anything of the kind. It is not my purpose to try to prevent the holding of that conference. I believe in joint industrial councils in Canada, and I want this conference to proceed. I shall vote gladly for the appropriation of the amounts necessary to the holding of that conference. All I ask is that it be more representative. I admit that it is late to change what has been done, but I wish to lay down a principle to this House: what I ask is representation of all labour, especially of all organized labour, all labour belonging to any union, at all labour conferences held in this country.
I have endeavoured, Sir, to put the situation clearly before the House. Is there anything in it which justifies the strong words employed by the Minister of Labour and the denunciation which he made, speaking for the Government? for he took the trouble to say that he was speaking for the Government. Was there any political trick on my part on agreeing to introduce to the minister the officers of the National Union, not even knowing what resolutions they were going to submit to him? Did
[Mr. Lapointe.}
the Government support the Minister of Labour in this attitude? They are, of course, responsible for his words and actions. Moreover, the Minister of Labour stands high in the councils of the Government. I have in my hand the Labour Gazette of October 20, in which is reported a speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) before the Trades and Labour Congress at Windsor. The Prime Minister is reported at page 1333, to have said speaking of the Government:
It has taken from the ranks of organized labour a vice-president of one of its largest organizations and has given him Cabinet rank. Never has a Labour Minister in Canada been accorded a more generous confidence from his colleagues and a freer hand in the administration of labour problems than has Senator Gideon Robertson. There is no department that requires ability of a higher type. A practical labour man, for the first time in our history, has been in charge, and after two years' trial I believe the almost universal feeling of Canada is that he has discharged his task with admirable fairness and with extraordinary capacity. He has done honour to the ranks from which he came and has compelled the confidence of men and women of every class.
Senator Robertson's policy has been to work in co-operation with responsible labour organizations and with organizations of employers as well.
Surely my right hon. friend did not know at that time the attitude of the Minister of Labour with regard to the National Labour Union which I should consider, and I think he should consider, to be a responsible labour organization.
The two other members of the triumvirate, Robertson, Moore and Draper, in making the statements they made, utterly misrepresented the facts. When Mr. Moore stated, in the speech which I have mentioned, that the National Union came to Ottawa and asked that it supersede the International Union at the conference and before the Government, he stated what was absolutely untrue. When the National Union asked for one member or two members at that conference out of a membership of thirty, was that a demand for superseding the International Union? Let me tell Mr. Moore that it is only a question of justice that I am defending now, and when National Unions want to supersede International Union, as he says, I shall be behind Mr. Moore, or perhaps a little ahead of him, to defend the rights of the International Union. It is no wonder, when such statements and speeches are made, that resolutions may be passed at those meetings; but those who voted for those resolutions are not acquainted with the facts; they are being deceived, as the hearers

of Mr. Moore were deceived when they passed that resolution.
The attitude of Mr. Moore and Mr. Draper may be quite comprehensible. They are not few in Canada, especially in the ranks of labour, of international labour at that, who believe that Messrs. Robertson, Moore and Draper are ruling labour in an autocratic manner and desire to perpetuate by all means their domination and arbitrary methods. Either one or the other is, a member of some commission or committee or board, and they do not relish the idea that some one else from some other organization should be recognized and should have a share of influence. This condition is not to the personal disadvantage of these gentlemen. They are travelling extensively at the expense of the country. Volume 2 of the Auditor General's Report shows that Mr, Moore, during the last fiscal year, has been a recipient of public money on a large scale. At page M-15 of that report, I see with regard to the Industrial Relations Commission, the following item:
Tom Moore, Ottawa, commissioner; services, 69 days at $20 ; travelling expenses, $700, total, $2,080.
At page M-17, I see the following item:
International Labour Conference, Paris and Washington, Tom Moore, president, Trades and Labour Congress of Canada: subsistence allowance, 84 days at $20 ; travelling expenses and disbursements, $594.20 ; less allowance from International Labour Office for attendance at London meeting, $818.35; total, $1,455.85.
A little later on I see, with regard to the Washington conference, apart from a substantial amount received by my friend Mr. Draper:
Tom Moore, $614.43.
Thus members of the House will see that Mr. Moore, apart from his salary as president of the Trades and Labour Congress, is receiving a fine share of the public money of this country, and it is not surprising that he wants to keep as much as possible for himself the hen that lays the golden eggs.
As regards Mr. Draper, everybody knows that, besides being an employee of this Government with a good salary-and I am told that he got a promotion after the Windsor meeting of the Trades and Labour Congress of last fall-Mr. Draper travels extensively throughout the world as representative of labour appointed by the department, and he has been receiving a fair share of public money. In that connection, I am not sure whether it is quite proper that an employee of the Government should act in that dual capacity. I am not alone in suggesting
that. I read in a very important British Review, the New Statesmen of February 5, 1921, at page 526:
At one time it looked as if the Labour party might play a notable part in the evolution now in process, but it is rent by internal quarrels and its leadership is miserably ineffective. Mr. Tom Moore, the president of the Trades and Labour Congress, has many good qualities, but lacks vigorous initiative and belief in the efficacy of political action. However, the prime source of weakness of the Labour movement lies in the fact that his second-in-command, the secretary of the congress, holds a fat civil service position in Ottawa.
I know that there are many in the Labour movement who do not like this condition of things. In the Toronto Globe of September 15, 1920, I find a report on the deliberations of the Trades and Labour Congress from which I take the following excerpt :
President Tom Moore refused to accept a resolution from delegates of the Toronto Labour Council to-day, when the convention opened, which called for the appointment of a special committe to investigate the disposition of $50,000 which Allan Barker, former president of the International Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees, is said to have sent Mr. Draper to use to fight radical propaganda in Canada. The few radicals who are in the convention had hoped to make capital out of the charge.
"I shall have to rule this out of order," said President Moore. "First, because it carries with it a veiled insinuation. If this were sent broadcast over the country it would give the impression that a charge was pending against Mr. Draper. Then, we have been advised by the [DOT] maintenance of way employees that their internal affairs should not be discussed by the Congress. It says that there can be no charge against Mr. Draper and that it is satisfied with his conduct."
Mr. Barker is charged with the misappropriation of funds of the brotherhood and his case will be heard shortly in Detroit.
It was said in the evidence at the trial that $50,000 of the funds of that association had been sent to Mr. P. M. Draper to fight radical propaganda. There are many in the Labour movement who believe that Mr. Draper and his friends thought that the best way to fight radical propaganda was to use those funds to insure their re-election as president and secretary of the Trades and Labour Congress.
As to the Minister of Labour, I shall have very little to say. I shall not even attempt to correct his misrepresentations with regard to myself. I can claim that I am fully as good a friend of Labour as he is. We both have had our hour of trial. When Senator Robertson was in Winnipeg at the time of the great strike, siding openly with the employers, and taking the

humiliating step of sending a frantic appeal to Samuel Gompers, the 5 p.m. head of the American Federation of Labour, to come and settle the difficulty out there, I was here on the floor of the House defending the rights of Labour to collective bargaining. When the Canadian National Railway Company was organized I took the responsibility of presenting the claims of Labour to representation on the Board of Directors, and the Government opposed my request with the implicit support and on the responsibility of the Minister of Labour. I desire to say as firmly as I can that by the attitude which the Minister of Labour has taken in the question I have been discussing, he has demonstrated that he is utterly unfit and entirely disqualified to occupy the high position of Minister of Labour in Canada. A Minister of Labour must be practicable in his plans, logical in his arguments, and absolutely fair and consistent in his undertakings. Above all, he must be impartial in his dealings with all sections of labour, organized and unorganized; all workmen must be equal before his department. The present Minister of Labour has proven that he lacks these elementary qualifications. He has shown himself devoid of the gift of tact, devoid of that broadmindedness and diplomacy which are necessary to achieve success in his department. Indeed, he has exhibited a deplorable lack of common sense. I have been told by people who are friendly to him that he did not realize the full extent of the responsibility he had as Minister of Labour, and I am fair enough to believe that that is true. But, Sir, that is no reason for keeping him there; it is no reason for the Government taking responsibility for his actions. I am sure that his actions in that respect are caused less by ill-will than

Mr. Speaker, I should like to use a polite substitute for the word ignorance.
That is all I have to say to-day. In closing my remarks I repeat what I have already said, that I base my arguments only and solely on the principle of justice, believing in the righteousness of the cause which I have defended, and believing that that is all-sufficient in the eyes of a population who love justice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject on
which the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has treated the House to quite a lengthy speech is one that most of us, in some of its features, would like to 
have introduced in Parliament as seldom as possible. It has not always proved practicable that it be wholly excluded from discussion in this chamber, and all that one can ask when such discussions must come, is that they be conducted with temper and moderation, and with scrupulous regard for the feelings of one's opponents.
The hon. member for Quebec East has sought to impugn, though his conclusions did not take the form of any resolution or amendment, the general administration for the Minister of Labour, and the basis of his charge is the conduct of that minister in relation to a certain application made by officers of a Catholic union in Canada for representation at a conference to be held in Ottawa next month. With a skill which undoubtedly the hon. member has developed to quite a height, he has succeeded most triumphantly in confusing the issue by a long statement of utterly impregnable principles, all the while assuming that one or other of these principles had been flagrantly violated by the minister. A more exact, careful and complete recital of the real circumstances in order to lay before Parliament just what the minister did, under what circumstances he acted and why he gave the decision that he did, would, I think, have been more appropriate than many of the lengthy extracts which the hon. member read.
Possibly a brief review of the Labour situation in Canada may be necessary to a full understanding of this matter. I do not pretend that I can speak with the amplitude of detail, or perhaps with the firmness of confidence in my facts that others could, hut if I am wrong, I ask to be corrected on the spot.
Labour organizations in Canada have existed almost since the Confederation of Canada. We have here members of international unions in very large numbers, and we have numbers of unions that are wholly ' Canadian. These, for the most part, are represented in what is known as the Trades and Labour Congress, which is a congress of Canadian representatives of these unions created for the purpose of watching and, to the best of their capacity, influencing legislation along lines they believe to be in their interests. There has grown up also since 1911 what are known as National Catholic Unions, confined, so far as I know, to the province of Quebec, unions composed wholly of catholics and adopting constitutions differing, in this respect, entirely from those adopted by other unions. These have reached considerable numbers

in that province. The constitution adopted by one of these unions is quoted in the letter of the Minister of Labour, read by the hon. member when he presented his case.	i
Now, those unions which are represented in the Trades and Labour Congress are constituted on what is known as the craft basis; that is to say, all the members of a craft join together for union purposes, for the sake of advancing their interests, and for wide co-operative objects. There is within these unions no distinction of race, religion, or anything else; the only basis of union is occupation in a craft. All are treated alike and have the same rights. The National Catholic Unions in the province of Quebec have been organized along different lines. I do not say that it was not their right so to do; I have not the least doubt that it was quite legal. At all events, they have organized along different lines and are in no way associated with the unions that form part of the Trades and Labour Congress. They have indeed taken the position, as set out in the letter quoted by the hon. member, that they have no relation to, and nothing to do with, the unions that are reflected and represented in the Trades and Labour Congress, nor with the Trades and Labour Congress itself. That position also is within their right, and there is no need to take exception to it, for it has nothing to do with the arguments and the facts before the House to-day. I stated that the National Catholic Unions sprang up in 1911. They have grown in numbers until in 1920 their strength, I believe, is claimed to be 39,712. They embrace many persons who could not be properly described as workmen. Many of these unions are really not, in the strict sense, labour unions, although a great many others are. Some of them consist of what are known as research clubs; I have the names of one or two, such as "The Pius X Research Club, of Levis," and "The Leo XIII Research Club, of Quebec"; and others. Of that 39,712, I understand only about 700 are actually engaged in the building trades.
The Trades and Labour Congress, of course, represents some hundreds of thousands. If my recollection of the memorandum presented me is correct, the members of the unions in the Trades and Labour Congress from the the province of Quebec total 89,000 or 90,000. While I do not think it matters as to the religious denominations of these 90,000 men in the Province of
Quebec who are in unions represented in the Trades and Labour Congress, it must be manifest to all who know anything of that Province that by that by far a larger number of catholics will be in those unions than could be in the catholic unions, whose total membership is only 39,000. Consequently, it will be difficult to argue that, while an attitude might be unfair to one or other, a preference for either on the part of the present Minister of Labour must necessarily arise from any narrow or anti-catholic impulse. No one who knows that minister would for a moment suppose that he is capable of being animated by any such feeling. The one motive that actuates him most is a real sympathy for Labour, particularly for Canadian labour and union labour. That is what is deepest in his heart,-a desire to advance the interests of all labour in this country, and his sympathies are strongly with the workers of our country, tempered, of course, by a spirit of fairness and a loftiness of view that well comport with his position and that have been, in the years he has occupied his present office,-yes, and for years before,-of inestimable service to this country.
That being the general labour position, how does it come about that the present difficulty arises? I have set out that the Catholic unions exist; I have set out that the other unions also exist; and I have shown the distinction that obtains between the two. Now, I would never for a moment argue from that state of facts that there could be taken up on the part of the Government of this country, or of the Labour Department, a position which denied recognition to the one or the other. That is obviously an impossible position for the Government or the Labour Department to take. Nor has that department been guilty of refusing recognition to either. I .purpose reciting the facts to show the truth of what I assert; many of the facts and some of the correspondence which he overloked might well have been submitted by the hon. member; but they would never at all have agreed with the conclusion at which he arrived, that there was failure on the part of the minister of any general recognition, or indeed of any specific recognition, that could, on logical grounds have been requested. What was the recognition asked for? It was in this respect, I think, that the hon. gentleman erred most. I think he led the House to believe that the officers of the Federation of National Catholic Unions

came to Ottawa, accompanied by himself, to make	a	general	request
for recognition, as he put it, on all commissions and, I think he said, on conferences appointed by the Government. If they came for purposes that were reasonable they would not have been denied. If they came for recognition in respect of anything they could fairly claim to be represented in they would not have been denied. What they specifically came for was this: A conference had been called on the part of two parties to an agreement. Now who were those parties? There has grown up in Canada, on the one hand, an organization known as the Federal Association of Building Trades, composed of various unions in different parts of Canada, who have got together, for purposes that I shall set out. On the other hand there has grown up an organization known as the Federal Association of Builders and Contractors-that is to say an association of the employers who employ the men-aggregated together in the other associations. An agreement was made some time ago between these two parties and out of that agreement real results have come. These results have been chiefly along the line of the establishment of Industrial Councils, at specific points through the country, between the employees in the building trades on the one hand- members of the General Association-and the employers members of the Employers' Association, on the other. There has evolved as well what you might call a Central Industrial Council-I think they call it an Industrial Conference'-composed of five who are named by the various employees organizations, parties to the agreement on the one hand, and of five more named by the employers' organization, parties to the agreement on the other hand. Now it was desired by the two parties to that agreement that a conference should be held, in the belief that difficulties that might loom up in the future, ana that they saw on the horizon, might be solved and smoothed away, and in the belief, I understand, that it would promote the further establishment and further usefulness of these Industrial Councils. That was the conference that was asked by these men-organized on the one hand, by the employees; organized by the employers on the other. Does any hon. gentleman know why that conference should not have been held? Does any hon. member know why these parties to a distinct individual agreement should be denied the right of having representatives come together for the purpose of ex-
changing their views? Does any hon. member know why the Minister of Labour should not have acquiesced in the demand for the assistance of his department when the parties came together for the purpose of calling that conference? If no one knows of any such reasons then there can be no criticism of the Minister of Labour.
What was the assistance asked of the Department of Labour? Was it that the minister should name the parties of either side to come to the conference? No, it was merely this-that in the case of this conference of the two parties to the agreement in question he should send the invitations to their nominees, and that he himself, or some officer of his department, should preside at the conference when held -the conference called for the 3rd of May. When matters were in that position a delegation came from the Federation of National Catholic Unions-those 39,000 people odd, of whom only 700 odd were in the building trades and none of whom were in the organizations represented by the employers who were a party to the agreement, and certainly none of whom were members of the employers' organization which constituted the second party to the agreement. They came down, and they came down accompanied by the hon. member for Quebec East. It was not the first time the members of this organization had come, but whenever they came they were welcome. I will read in a little while something that took place at a previous meeting between the representatives of the National Catholic Unions and the Minister of Labour. I will quote the verbatim report of what took place; and I say now that it will show to the hon. member for Quebec East and to every member of this House that the stand which the hon. member advocated looking to the smooth working together and co-operation of the Trades and Labour Congress on the one hand and of the Federation of Catholic Unions on the other-the stand which he says it is the great business of the Minister of Labour to take-is precisely the stand that the Minister of Labour did assume.

speechtext: Not this year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The question is not up this year; that is not what they came down for. They came down accompanied by the member for Quebec East although they had with them before-I do not know just how to refer to the gentleman but I want to do so in a correct way-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The Chaplain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Yes the Chaplain,
Abbe Fortin. He was down in 1920 at the head of the delegation, but this time they required the member for Quebec East to introduce them. So the hon. member came with them to the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I suppose my right
hon. friend will take my word when I say I was invited to go there without at all knowing what the resolutions were going to be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I do not doubt that at all. What I said was the delegation brought the hon. member with them and he introduced them although they were accompanied by the gentleman who led them in 1920. That is the fact. I do not say the hon. member knew the purport of the resolutions; I accept his word instantly when he says he did not. Anyway he came with them, and I believe another member of this House came with them as well.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Was there any wrong in that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
No, I do not say there was anything wrong. I would be the last to argue that it was wrong on the part of an hon. member to take advantage of every such occasion in his public life. Every hon. member wants to get behind him all the strength he can; I simply call attention to the grounds upon which he came. Now that is of interest when I go on a little further. I have stated the specific object for which they came. Did hon. members of this House get that to be the specific object from the speech of the hon. member? I do not think they did. The request of the delegation was denied by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Labour took this ground: How can I say to these people who have the right to make their own nominations, "You must see to it that somebody else comes to this conference between these two said parties to the said agreement; I won't allow you to have that conference unless you do"? Had he the right to take that ground? I think my hon. friend knows he had not, and must have known it, especially in view of the fact that of the delegation which he introduced, representing 39,000 odd people, only 700 odd were in the building trades, whereas the parties to the conference were wholly of the building trade. Yet in spite of that the delegation asked the Minister of Labour to take the situation strongly in hand and say to
these two parties to the agreement "You cannot get together unless the other parties come in as well." Was that a fair request to make? And after the Minister of Labour had stated his views, I am informed, and I am informed by the Minister of Labour himself, that the labour representatives present-those of the delegation who were themselves labouring people- did not take any exception to those views and that the opposition was first taken bv the hon. member for Quebec East himself,

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Who says that?
