maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Labour.	The	Minister	of

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
The	Minister	of
Labour is stating an untruth when he			says
that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I had better repeat it so that it will be understood. My information from the minister is that the labour delegates there, those who were labouring people, did not take exception to his statement of the position when he refused to himself compel representation at the conference, but that the first to take exception was the hon. member for Quebec East.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I insist upon my right to have my word accepted by the right hon. gentleman. The Minister of Labour could not understand the men who were there, and I had to translate to him what they were saying.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Order. The Prime
Minister has not refused to accept the statement of the hon. member. It is perfectly proper for the Prime Minister to state what the Minister of Labour said to him in respect to a certain occasion. What the hon. member has said in this House must be accepted. That is the rule of the House. His word is on record and will stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Now we have reached that point of the argument. The Minister of Labour did not take the stand he did in relation to refusing the request on the ground that this was a Catholic union, or that he had any fault to find with it. He took his stand on the ground that I have stated-a ground that I humbly submit, is utterly unassailable. I cannot for the life of me see how he could possibly have taken any other stand. I say he did not take that stand on the ground that he had to treat differently the workingmen engaged



in the building trade who happened to be members of a union who were parties to the conference and members engaged in the same trade who happened to be members of the Catholic union; not at all. On the contrary he stated: This is a conference between these two parties to an agreement which they have a right to hold, and they have a right to determine the way in which they will hold that conference. They have determined how they will hold it, and I have no right to interfere, especially as the unions you represent are not building trades unions particularly but only to the extent of two per cent of your members. What followed from that? Instead of trying to discriminate in favour of one as against the other, he followed that statement with a letter, which the hon. member did not read. I have the letter before me and will read it now.
Mr. J. E. A. Pin,
270 rue de la Reine,
Quebec, Que.
I presume he is the secretary of the union or of the delegation.
Ottawa, Ont., March 29, 1921.
Dear Sir,- The proposals contained in the printed memorial and submitted by your delegation last week have been translated and are receiving consideration. One of the requests made referred to a conference to be held in Ottawa on May 3 next, and to be participated in by employers and representatives of labour parties to the National Builders Industrial Council agreement.
Parties to the agreement.
You will recall it was explained to your delegation that the delegates to this conference were not being selected or appointed by the Department of Labour, but at the request of the employers' and workmen's organizations, parties to the Industrial Council agreement, the department had agreed to invite the delegates whom the respective parties might nominate.
Upon the occasion of the visit of your delaga-tion it .was made clear to them that the department could not assume to force upon the employers' and employees organizations, parties to the Industrial Council agreement, the presence of outside organizations of either employers or workmen, but that if your organization would communicate directly with the parties who were participating in the conference and obtain their consent to your being represented, it would be the pleasure of the department to extend invitations to any members of your organization who might be nominated.
That is what he stated to the delegation. I do not think the hon. member quoted that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: He never said that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: He did not state that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
No; and it is not in
the letter he wrote to the Montreal Gazette.
fMr. Meighen..]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I think it is in that
letter. If so, I do not know where the hon. member will be then. But the Minister of Labour did not stop there. In his letter to this gentleman, who I think must be the secretary of the delegation, he also said:
Since then it has occurred to me that your people have perhaps overlooked the fact that the employers in the building industry who engage only National Catholic Union workers will not be present at the conference referred to. If in the opinion of your organization, and of the employers with whom your organization deals, it would be advisable to have a conference together, similar to the one to be held between employers and employees, members oi * the national building industrial council, it will be the pleasure of the Department of Labour to extend invitations, upon receipt of nominations, in exactly the same manner as is being done in the other case.
If a conference between the bui-lding contractors, who employ members of your organization only, and yourselves, is deemed desirable the department will be glad to co-operate with you in exactly the same manner as we are attempting to do with the other organizations of builders and workmen.
Now, I do not say that the hon. member ever had seen this letter before he spoke-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Is the right hon. gentleman reading the whole letter or just extracts?,	.	'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
No, I have read the
whole letter. The latter part of the letter in which it is suggested that possibly the workmen in Mr. Pin's organization would like a similar conference with their employers, the minister does not claim to have stated to the delegates. He did tell them what is expressed in the first part, that if Mr. Pin's organization would obtain the consent of the parties interested to his organization being represented, he-(the minister)-would be glad to extend invitations,-in a word, if justice was being done by the parties to the conference, they who were not parties would be treated precisely the same even in relation to that conference. What more the Minister of Labour could do I am at a loss to understand.
Now the hon. member complains that the Minister of Labour has not taken the line of seeking to avoid friction between the Catholic unions and the unions incorporated in the Trades and Labour Congress. I say, on the contrary, that the minister has taken precisely that line, and has always taken it. He has felt that friction was bound to arise when organization took place along those lines. He has felt that it is better for labour to be all together, to present its case as one, not as two. He has

always tried to get them together but his efforts have not received much response, and I know he feels discouraged by the attitude of those whose cause the hon. member has espoused this afternoon.
Now let me read what took place a year ago at this meeting between the representatives of the Federation of National Catholic unions and the Minister of Labour. This is a verbatim report of what he said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Would the
Prime Minister allow me to correct one impression before he proceeds? He has made reference to a letter which my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) is not supposed to have seen. As my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has realized, the speech of the member for Quebec East had reference to a letter from the Minister of Labour which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on March 31. The delegates are being invited upon the nomination of the employers' and workmen's respective organizations. The National Catholic Union delegates would be gladly invited if the consent of the parties participating were obtained, but instead of approaching them the National Catholic Union make a demand on the Labour Department to force representation for them, which request was declined. Why did the National Cathoi/ic Union make this request instead of seeking to co-operate with the two parties interested ?

speechtext:
No, 1920. The minister said:
If I may be permitted-and I hope you will not regard it as presumption on my part- to call one or two things to your attention, for the consideration of your federation, and it is for the purpose of promoting harmonious relations in the labour world and in the industrial world generally that I presume to advance these thoughts for your consideration.
There have been established in the province of Quebec during the last few years what you have been pleased to term your National Catholic Unions. I had the pleasure and honour of being received by Bishop Gauthier and several other gentlemen, including Father Fortin, in Montreal some ' weeks ago to discuss some of the things that I am going to mention now. Throughout all of the rest of Canada, and indeed all Northern America, the wage earners, the workingmen, are organized into what they term their craft unions. That is, the carpenters have their organization; the machinists have theirs; the boilermakers have

theirs; the street railway men have theirs; each class of men in railroad service have their particular organization; and the bricklayers, the stonemasons, the garment-workers, etc. Those organizations are all, or nearly all, international in character. That may or may not be a good thing, but what I want to point out in the first place is that there is no distinction as to any race, nationality or creed in that whole labour movement numbering several millions of people. The movement that has started in your province, setting up what is termed the National Catholic Unions, is having a very disturbing effect in the minds of labour men generally-those who are affiliated with these other unions that have been in existence for years-particularly in your province; and unfortunately it is true that the feeling is not all of a friendly sort. I think that it is unfortunate that there should be any friction between men whose interests are identical. But if you continue to increase your membership- in the province of Quebec among your own people, and the friction continues to grow by reason of certain provisions in your constitution, which may be misunderstood, misquoted, and misinterpreted in other parts of the Dominion, I honestly greatly fear that serious results will ultimately come out of what has been started, and I would like to make this suggestion to you gentlemen here. You have placed a number of important matters before 'Mr. Blondin and myself on behalf of the Government, for consideration by the Government, and I am therefore going to venture to ask you to give consideration to the proposal that I desire to make to you. It is that you should honestly and earnestly endeavour to find some method whereby your organization can work in more complete haimony with the other organizations representing labour in this country, and at least stop the growing friction that exists. Father Fortin was present when we had the conversation in Montreal, and we need not discuss the matter at the length we did there, because he is familial* with it; but I do respectfully submit, gentlemen, that there ought to be no religious distinction in the labour movement. In every trades union that exists in North America, Catholic and Protestant are alike welcome, and have equal rights, and the question of religion is never raised. The * secretary of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada is a most devout Roman Catholic; several of the executive of that congress are also of that religious faith, and they have the confidence and the admiration and the respect of their fellow workmen of all religious beliefs throughout the whole country, for they are elected by them.	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Minister-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
And what I wanted to say was that I do hope that as you proceed along your line of development you will earnestly endeavour to promote more harmonious relations between other organizations and your own, both your local unions and ypur federation, and if possible adopt the same principle that we are suggesting should be adopted between employer and employee, namely, by getting together with the executive officials of the other unions and endeavouring by conference to find some common ground on which you can work together in harmony.
That is exactly the policy which the hon. member Hays the Minister of Labour should promote.

Do not have them coming to me or to the Government-no matter who may happen to be Minister-and saying, "We won't participate in the Labour Conference if another organization is present." It is undesirable to have one organization representing labour coming to the Government and saying, "We want the eight hour day," and another organization coming and saying, "We do not." Unless there is harmony and unity of action, the Government is placed in a most embarrassing position in dealing with the presentations that are made. The Government has even been endeavoring, and with some success, to get labour and capital to sit down, talk together, and bring in joint recommendations. That is very desirable and has been useful where it has been done. Everything possible should be done to bring about a spirit of co-operation among all the organizations that are trying to improve the condition of the workingman in any part of this country. I think it is desirable that they should be pulling together instead of having any differences, and coming at different times and making opposite representations to the Government in some cases. I do not mean the remarks that I have made to be taken as in any way offensive, as I am sure you gentlemen will appreciate. I lived in the province of Quebec for some six years, and knew a great many of the people there and Lave great admiration for the French people. It is unfortunately true that in the distant parts of Canada our French-Canadian people are not properly understood, and in many cases not properly appreciated. Their ideas and aims are somewhat different from those of , other people in other parts of the Dominion. At the same time I believe that it is absolutely true, on the other hand, that the majority of our people in the province of Quebec, do not fully understand the people in the other provinces of Canada. It is only by the meeting of representatives of all parts of the country, whether of labour or capital, that we become properly possessed of the right ideas, the ideas that should prevail for the benefit of the country as a whole. So I leave that thought with you for your consideration.
This is what I want to emphasize particularly.	.
If at any time it seems to your Federation desirable that a conference should be held between officers of your organization and officers of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, with a view of trying to arrive at some common ground on which you can work together in harmony, or at least so work that friction -would be avoided, and if this Department can be of any service in bringing about such a conference, we would be delighted to co-operate with you in that way.
Even the words of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lapointe) himself could not more clearly or more forcefully express the devotion that a minister ought to show to the cause of co-operation amongst labour, to the cause of the abolition of that friction amongst labour classes, and especially of the abolition of friction that involves from religious division.
The hon. member must realize that, in so far as any administrative decision went, the decision of the Minister of Labour as

regards this question of being represented at this special council was specifically, the only administrative decision that he made. But when the hon. member (Mr. Lapointe) got up to charge him with discrimination, he gave, as he expressed it to me, " without cost," his opinion. The Minister of Labour has opinions as to the wisdom of organizing workers along the special line, the religious line, such as at the basis of this Catholic Union. It is not that the Minister of Labour is anti-Catholic. His opinion would be just the same as regards the organization for labour purposes adherents of any other religious body in Canada, It would be just the same as regards a clerical party in this House of any religious denomination whatever. Such is the opinion; it is not an administrative act at all. The Minister of Labour, so far as administrative direction goes, takes the ground that in his eye all must be treated alike; there must be no refusal to recognize anyone. But he believes that the best line of labour organization is not the line that marks the confines of a religious sect. That is his opinion; surely to that opinion he has a right, and the opinion applies to such an organization, no matter by what special religious boundary it may be confined. I will give you his reasons. He states that in his experience as a labour man, as Minister of Labour, the inevitable result of workers organizing on religious lines is to give ground for complaints of discrimination and unfairness on the part of employees, Catholic or Protestant, who cannot or do not belong to this Catholic Union so organized or to this special organization of labour within lines of particular faith. In his judgment there inevitably arise claims of injustice to those men who do not, who cannot, belong because they are in other unions or because they are not Catholics. Furthermore he holds this opinion on the far broader ground, namely that the projection of lines of division amongst our people on religious grounds into the labour field-and I think he would say into other fields-is not for the ultimate good of Canada. That is his opinion. But because he believes that it would be better to organize along other lines that is no reason why he should not recognize organizations if they choose to take form, so long as such organizations are within, and entitled to the protection of, the laws of this country and so long as the purpose of the organization is in no way destructive. That being his position, what fault can be found?
There is, however, an organization of another character that arose in the West, and in the judgment of the minister it had much to do with the Winnipeg strike. I am rather sorry to see the hon. member trying to lead the House to believe to-day that in the great conflict that arose in Winnipeg, his sympathies were wholly with those who precipitated that struggle there, some of whom were found guilty of grave crimes by unanimous verdicts of juries. I did not know that the hon. member would stand in this House and say that he was pleading their cause here when the Minister of Labour was in the West trying to restore order in one of the most trying and difficult situations that ever arose in Canada. I did not believe that he would stand in Parliament and try to prove his claim to sympathy with labour on any reasoning like that. I do not think that these grounds he will get very much sympathy from leading members of his party, whose views on. that occasion were expressed quite freely, honestly, honourably and truly, quite on the other side.
I have described the position that the minister took; the position that he outlines in his letter to the Montreal Gazette. That position is wholly compatible with his lifelong effort to bring about the best possible relations between labour units as they appear in the Trades and Labour Congress and labour units as they appear in the Catholic union, and quite consistent with that policy, from which he has never departed, of recognizing the one in the same way as he would recognize the other and in giving no preference to either. That is the position he has assumed all along. In that position, is he wrong? In that position, I venture to say he is supported by the majority, even of the religious faith of those who belong to the Catholic unions, and by the majority of labour men. I know it is his firm opinion that the majority do support him in that position, and I think he is a competent judge as to what side the majority are on. In that position I have not the least doubt that he is supported by the great body of fair, impartial, unbiased public opinion in this country; and in pursuing that course I think he is serving the ends of labour, the ends of the Dominion, and deporting himself with dignity and usefulness in the high office which he holds.
At Six o'clock, the House took recess.

After Recess

speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in my remarks, for on no account would I spoil the good impression made upon this House by the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). I had the honour to accompany the delegates of the National Labour Union when they called upon the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson); I heard all the proposals which were submitted to him; I heard their request which was to be presented at the industrial conference of employers and workmen, in Ottawa, on May 3rd next; a conference called by the hon. minister himself, and having for its object the bringing together of employers and employees with a view to securing a better understanding between them. They solicited the favour to send three of the thirty-seven delegates who will make up the conference, that is to say a quota proportionate to the 50,000 workmen they represented. Much to my surprise, Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Labour, forgetting that he is the Minister of Labour for the whole country, whatever be the union to which they belong, refused their request, for the reason that these men are members of a Catholic National union. And here I mean to state, that the minister does not tell the truth when he says that the only protest against his refusal was that from the member for Quebec East. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Quebec East only served as an interpreter for the benefit of the Minister of Labour who does not understand French, and the delegates warmly protested, but in vain, as the minister's refusal was final.
When one looks over the political history of this country one encounters many politicians and other groups mixed up in intrigues having for their object to discredit all that is Catholic. I still remember the wars waged against Sir Wilfrid Laurier by certain fanatics; I have many times heard them say that they wanted no Prime Minister who received his directions from Rome and the pope, or other similar nonsense, but never before have I seen a minister of the Crown, supposed to represent all races and creeds of the country, forget himself to the extent of sinking to the level of the fanatical politicians I have just referred to. And this happens, Mr. Speaker, at the very moment when the Government try to have ministers elected in the province of Que-

bee, and tell us through their newspapers that they want friendly understanding and union to prevail in the country, and that they even regret not to see our province better represented in the Cabinet. I remember the account given of a grand banquet offered to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) in Montreal, where he declared that he had never uttered a word or sentence that could offend the province of Quebec. Well, Mr. Speaker, here is a fact which speaks louder than mere words, and if the Prime Minister be sincere, if he wants us to believe in his courting, let him repudiate the conduct of his colleague, the Minister of Labour, and demand his resignation.
After all, why this objection to the Catholic labour unions? Is it not admitted by everybody that it was the province of Quebec that saved the situation, that put an end to the friction which after the war existed in this country between capital and labour? Indeed, when strikes were taking place in all the provinces of the Dominion -I still have in mind the famous strike in Winnipeg-the province of Quebec was calm and peaceful and was the bulwark of order and harmony. Mr. Speaker, the reason is that the people, especially the working classes, are permeated with deep religious sentiments and follow the wise and patriotic advice of their clergy. Although the honourable Minister of Labour is adverse to the presence of a chaplain among trades unions, I wish to state on the floor of this House that as long as they follow the advice of the clergy our workingmen will not go astray and Quebec will be admired by the people of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few days ago-last Sunday it was-I had the good fortune to be present at a gathering called under the auspices of the National Catholic Unions of Labour in the city of Quebec. At this meeting held in the Market hall there were about three thousand people present, and many more were unable to get in. This large number of people had gathered to hear a very prominent member of the clergy, Abbe Deponcheville. He addressed this gathering of Catholic Labour Unions and I must say that I was very much impressed with his speech, as I believe everybody present was on that occasion. Did he say anything against other labour unions? No. Did he say anything particularly in favour of Catholic unions? Possibly so.

When I left that room I asked myself, how are we going to face the situation which now confronts us in view of what we had been told a few days previously by the Minister of Labour, the Hon. Gideon Robertson? Coming to Ottawa the next day, much to my surprise I received from people belonging to other labour unions a resolution which I wish to place in part before the House, the tenor of which was exactly to the contrary of what I had heard at the meeting I had attended the day previous. It is a resolution of the Quebec Typographical Union, No. 302, and says in part:	-
That whereas this Union has taken cognizance of the stand taken by the Hon. Gideon Robertson, Minister of Labour, in connection with the National Catholic Unions of this province in their efforts to divide bona fide labour organizations by means of religious and racial prejudice-
If it were true, Mr. Speaker, that the Catholic Unions want to divide bona fide labour organizations by means of religious and racial prejudice, I for one would by no means support any organization that would have any such tendency. I do not think the Catholic unions have any purpose of that sort in mind. The Abbe Fortin, who also spoke on this occasion, said that if Catholic unions wished to be advised by priests, it was their own business. He said further: We went to Ottawa for this very purpose of telling the Minister of Labour that whenever a labour congress took place, or a conference on labour matters was held, we wanted the Catholic unions of labour, representing over forty thousand people in this Dominion, to be heard. That was all. That was mentioned at that meeting by Abbe Fortin. He repeated there what he said in Ottawa that that was all the Catholic unions were trying to get from this Government.
The Minister of Labour has written a letter to the press, published in the Montreal Gazette, in which he tries to becloud the issue, saying that if the labour unions could not be heard at the coming congress it was because they were Catholic.
A day or so later another letter was published by the same gentleman, but he did not go quite so far as he did before. Now, it is our hope that whatever may be the nature of these organizations in the province of Quebec, whether they be advised by legal counsellors or by priests, they shall be given the same right to be heard by the Department of Labour as is enjoyed by any other union in Canada. There are
some forty thousand labour men in these Catholic unions, and they should have an opportunity of stating their views before any conference under the direction of the Minister of Labour. I will not go further on this subject because the whole field has been well covered by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), and everything that he has said concerning the whole matter I am pleased to endorse. I trust that the Government, taking his views into earnest consideration, and heeding the opinions expressed by some of us, will take such steps as will ensure to- these Catholic unions the right of being heard by the Department of Labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
It seems to me that the Labour Department is exercising a discrimination against the National Catholic Unions. There was a labour conference in September, 1919, at which those unions desired to be represented, but they were refused the right. Now, they serve a certain purpose in this country, and the Department of Labour should have no policy which would operate against the interests of any union of labour, whether its members belong to one denomination or another. Those Catholic unions want to be represented now at another labour conference, and they are denied the right by the Minister of Labour. Why is that? Are they not citizens of this country? They number about 40,000, and there is no reason why they should not be heard in any conference under the auspices of the Department of Labour. I wish to put on Hansard the views of a prominent labour man, who has had a large experience in the employment of labour in this country for the last thirty years. This man is not a Catholic; he is a Protestant named A. A. Wright, and writing from 9 Victoria Square, Montreal, under date of April 1; with reference to the National Catholic unions, he says:
To the Editor of The Gazette:
Sir,-I read with a great deal of interest yesterday your very able criticism of the position taken by the Minister of Labour, as shown by his letter in the same issue. It may be of interest to you to know that prior to' March, 1917, I had had over thirty years' experience in Ontario with unorganized labour in the lumber and shipping industries. During that period, the relations between the employing firm and * their employees were of the most friendly character, and nothing but harmony prevailed, mainly from the absence of paid agitators. From March, 1917, to date, I have been closely connected with firms from Port Arthur to Halifax, the first two years of that period being connected with the construction of patrol vessels in the shipyards from

Port Arthur to Quebec for the British Admiralty, under the Department of the Naval Service of Canada. This was my first experience with labor organizers or leaders of the Metal Trades Federation affiliated with the International Unions, whose activities are responsible for all the unrest in labor circles. It was my first connection also with the Catholic workers organization in the Province of Quebec.
I have no brief for the clergy of the Roman Catholic Church nor for the labor organization among members of that church, but I am compelled to state that from personal experience that if compelled to take my choice between dealing with the Catholic Workmen's Union or with the leaders of the International Unions, I would unquestionably prefer dealing with the Catholic Workers Union and their leaders for the following reasons:
The leaders and advisers of the Catholic Workmen's Union teach the workers to live up to the teachings of the Christian religion, and to give an honest day's work for a fair day's pay. They impress on the workers that the only source of employment is from the men who are able to use the savings of the people intelligently in producing commodities required by mankind, and that they can only pay the men the highest wages possible to them after paying for raw material, overhead expenses and a reasonable profit, and the difference between that, and the value of the commodities produced, is all that can possibly be available for wages.
On the other hand, the International Unions teach their members that the capitalist is the enemy of the workingman, who has been exploiting his services for the accumulation of wealth and not giving the worker a fair share of what he produces.
The International Unions, through some of their leaders, do admit that men should give an honest return for the wages they are paid, and when advocating the eight hour day guaranteed that if employers would grant the eight hour day, they would get greater production than they had been getting in the ten hour day. From observation in the industries with which I have been connected, instead of doing this the men have been giving, up to a few months ago, less than half of the production in eight hours which they had formel-y been giving in ten, because the workmen were privately, and in some cases openly taught, that the less work a man does the more men will get employment and the more prosperous workers will be. Further, I have been told by first class Union workmen, when asked why they belonged to a Union, since they were men of such a type that employers will bid against one another for their services, that they are virtually compelled to belong to the Union because there is an aggressive minority which, throught secret dealings with foremen and other means would drive them out of the shops if they incurred the enmity of the Unions and refused to join, because it is absolutely essential to the existence of the Unions that they have enrolled among their members a large number of skilled men, as without them the Union could not exist and these men are used to enable the indifferent and undesirable workmen to get and hold jobs.
I think it is safe to state that fully 80 per cent of the members of the labor unions are honest, conscientious, law-abiding citizens who take little or no interest in agitation, and that of the 201 per cent, of aggressive members,
[Mr. Proulx.I
possibly not over 5 per cent, are of the class which might be considered really undesirable citizens. When this is considered, coupled with the fact that organized labor affiliated with these International Unions does not embrace at the outside probably over 20 per cent, of all the workers in. Canada and the United States, it should be evident that too much attention is being paid to those so-called labor leaders (who arrogate to themselves the right to dictate through the press and public platforms to our Government as to what Labour demands), by the Government, press and public. They should be absolutely ignored, as if this country, or any other country, is to prosper, the Government elected by the people should only pass and administer laws for the benefit of all its citizens, instead of catering to a noisy minority by passing and enforcing laws for the benefit of a small minority of citizens at the expense of the majority.
I think a comparison of the ethics taught by the Catholic Workers Union leaders, and those of the International Unions, will justify the decision of many employers who after careful consideration now refuse to sign any contract with leaders of the International Unions, but will confine themselves to making agreements with men who are working for them who are willing to live up to their contracts, and give honest service in return for the highest wages which the firm can afford to pay.
A. A. Wright,
9 Victoria Cquare,
Montreal, April 1, 1921.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it has always been my opinion since the International Union entered upon an aggressive campaign against the National Catholic Union that the former wanted to kill the movement undertaken by the latter. They saw that in the province of Quebec the National Catholic Union was living up to the principles of the Christian religion in making-agreements with their employers and adhering to those agreements. You have not seen in the province of Quebec within the last few years any strikes worth speaking of, and even when strikes did occur they were very quickly settled. There has not been seen in the province of Quebec any such strike as the big one which occurred in the West. The members of the National Catholic Union are not members of the One Big Union. Nevertheless the Department of Labour has exercised discrimination in this matter, and I think the head of that department in so doing is acting at the dictation of the officers of the Trades and Labour Congress. I do not believe that the Minister of Labour wrote the letter which has been quoted here, I do not think he had the time to do so. I believe that letter was written by Mr. Tom Moore and Mr. P. M. Draper, the President and secretary respectively of the Trades and Labour Congress. The minister is taking

up the cudgels for these gentiemen and, I submit, acting unfairly towards the National Catholic Union. The members of that union number over 40,000. They are peaceful citizens who want to avoid strikes and to co-operate with their employers. We have heard much within the last few years about the necessity of having cooperation between employers and employees, and we cannot have industrial peace in this country without such co-operation. Well, the main principle of the National Catholic Union is that we should have co-operation along this line and they are carrying that principle into effect. If any employers who have made agreements with the members of the National Catholic Union were summoned and questioned before a committee of this House it would be found that all those employers are perfectly satisfied.
The Montreal Gazette is a very important newspaper, perhaps one of the most influential in the country, and in its utterances on this matter it knows whereof it speaks. That newspaper declares that the National Catholic Union should not be discriminated against and that it should be represented at any Labour Conference held in Canada, especially when the expenses of such a conference are met out of the public treasury. Has the International Union, I ask, any more right to come to this Parliament and ask that public money be devoted to meeting the expenses of a labour conference than the National Catholic Union? If the expenses of such a conference are met out of the public treasury, why should not the National Catholic Union be represented at it? My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was perfectly justified in accompanying the delegation that waited upon the Minister of Labour to ask that the minister recognize the National Catholic Union. I hope the Prime Minister will reconsider the decision arrived at in this matter; and I appeal to the Minister of Justice, who represents the province of Quebec in this House and who knows the membership and the principles of the National Catholic Union, to see that justice is done to them, and that they should be given representation at the forthcoming labour conference to be held in this city. I make this appeal hoping that the Minister of Justice will use his influence towards remedying the injustice which has been inflicted upon that organization.
Mr. HENRI E. LAVIGUEUR (Quebec County) :	If I may be permitted I would
like to say a few words on this subject. I have no intention of discussing the question at any length because my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has very ably placed all the facts before the House, supplemented by the hon. memhber for Quebec West (Mr. Parent). I wish to say, however, that I endorse absolutely every word which has been uttered by both these hon. gentlemen. The treatment which has been meted out to over 40,000 of the most peaceful and honourable working men of the province of Quebec constitutes a great insult to our race-it is not only an insult to the labour classes of that province but it is also an insult to our race and our religion. During the course of a great number of years I have had the advantage of observing the work of the National Catholic Union in the city of Quebec. I have had the honour and the pleasure of knowing the most of their officers, and on many occasions it has been my good fortune to meet with them touching labour matters in the city of Quebec not only during the war but subsequent to it. The members of the National Catholic Union of Quebec comprise some of the most honourable and worthy people we have. In the city of Quebec during and subsequent to the war there were never any labour troubles owing to the praiseworthy action of the National Catholic Union, to say nothing of the international union whose members also do good work in the interest of the trade and industry of the country. Under the circumstances I could not let the opportunity pass without saying that I endorse every word that has been uttered by hon. gentlemen on this side, and I would have been greatly pleased and happy had I been called upon to vote for a resolution asking the Minister of Labour to tender his resignation in the Cabinet. The Minister of Labour has no mandate from the people, he is simply responsible to the Government, and, I repeat, by his action in this matter he has insulted our people.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I do not wish to participate in
the debate, I merely want to ask a question. For that reason I am sorry the Prime Minister is not in his place. When he was speaking this afternoon I had in my mind to refer to it but did not wish to interrupt him. In putting the question now I am merely asking for information. I understood the Prime Minister to say that the proposed conference will not be a general labour conference, but a conference of two groups-one representing the workmen and

the other the employers in the building trades. I think that is correct. The Prime Minister further said that the Minister of Labour was not in a position to admit any other parties to the conference. I think that is correct also. Then the question arises: If two bodies of men desire to have a conference why do they bring the Minister of Labour into the matter at all, why do they come to him for his opinion? There are conferences all over Canada every week between employers and working men, but why is the Minister of Labour drawn into this disagreeable matter? Perhaps the Minister of Justice can answer the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Before the
Minister of Justice answers the question I would remind the hon. member that he has exhausted his right to speak, and that if he wishes to ask any further questions he had better do so now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I only desire to
ask one or two questions. I have stated the first one:	Why has the Government been
drawn into this matter, why could these parties not have their conference without bringing the Minister of Labour into the controversy? They did not need his permission. This conference, it appears to me, does not stand on any different basis from any other conference on the labour question in any part of Canada, and I cannot understand why the Minister of Labour and the Government are drawn into this very disagreeable matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I understand the position correctly, and I think I do, it is this. A body representative of a large number of working men in the building trade and another body representative of employers likewise in the building trade came to an agreement that with a view to adjusting difficulties, actual or anticipated, that might arise in connection with their relations it would be desirable to have a conference. They asked, as I understand it, that the Minister of Labour should furnish an officer of his department to act as chairman of that conference and, in a sense, to help bring the parties together.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Could they not come together?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
They certainly could
if they had thought proper to do so. But, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Quebec East this afternoon,-and I think

he read from the statutes-the function for which the Department of Labour exists is to do everything in its power to facilitate and further the getting together of employers and employees, and thereby to ensure the maintenance of peace and concord in our industrial operations. Whether these gentlemen who desire to have the conference were right or wrong in the view that it would promote concord between them, they did request what they thought would be helpful, and the Minister of Labour desiring to meet any expressed wish for such co-operation, agreed that an officer of his department should preside over this conference and should issue the invitations. I am not prepraed to say that it wag absolutely necessary, but it does seem to me that it was quite within the line of the duties of the Minister of Labour to meet such a request if it was at all possible to do so. I think that is the entire explanation of how the Department of Labour came to be connected with the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And, incidentally, the Government pay the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Incidentally the Government, I understand, do pay the expenses connected with this conference. But I leave it to this House whether, if conferences of this kind conduce to bringing about and maintaining a good understanding between employers and employees, it is not the proper function of the Ministry of Labour to encourage them and to co-operate with labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: To co-operate with all labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Yes. But when particular bodies representative of large numbers of men occupying towards each other the position of employers and employees represent to the department that a conference between them would be conducive to the results I have mentioned, even if they do not embrace the entire body of employers and employees throughout the country, is it not worth while to co-operate with those who seek to confer together and help them to that end?
Now, that is the whole explanation of the mystery, if there be a mystery connected with the matter. That being so, so long as the department offers and is ready to extend the same co-operation to any other body of employees and employers, it seems to me fairly clear that there can be no question of discrimination. But the difficulty seems to have resulted entirely

from a misapprehension on the part of the applicants of the nature of the conference in question. It has been said that I know something about the people that compose these Catholic unions. I do, and I believe that they are reasonable people, people that are not seeking to make trouble, and I cannot but believe that if they had fully understood that they were asking for representation, not at a general labour conference but at a conference between two particular bodies of men of which they did not form part, they would have realized that there was no intention to discriminate against them, and that they were not the victims of the injustice which the hon. member for Quebec East and possibly they themselves seemed to believe that they have been subjected to. I am confident that when the members of these unions come to understand the misapprehension under which they labour they will realize that there was no refusal of recognition and no injustice done to them. I think that was made abundantly clear by the offer to them of the same good services of the department if they thought there was any conference which they could have with their employers that would tend to produce the same results of good will and harmony.
I do not think there is any substantial difference of opinion about the principles that ought to govern this matter. The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) was quite in a postion to agree to the principles laid down by the hon. member for Quebec East. The difficulty seems to be that there was a misapprehension as to there having been a violation of those principles or a desire to ignore the particular request in question that led to the one administrative, action which took place. Surely, as the hon. member for Quebec East himself pointed out, the questions that may arise out of the correspondence he read are, after all, abstract questions upon which people may honestly differ in opinion, and, as he pointed out, each one is entitled to entertain his own opinions and to act upon them so long as he is within the law. The Minister of Labour, like everybody else, formed his opinions upon those abstract questions which, after all, do not arise here for us to discuss or de-, termine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Will my right hon.
friend allow me a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Will he take responsibility for what is stated in the letter written by the Minister of Labour to the Montreal Gazette?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I am just pointing out that for the opinions of the Minister of Labour upon those abstract questions I have no responsibility. I have a responsibility for the administrative actions of this Government, and in view of the explanation of the Prime Minister, what was done in this particular instance, nobody, I think, can question. There are doubtless many abstract questions upon which action is not called for on the part of this Government in connection with which I might not be in agreement with my friend the Minister of Labour, or, possibly, with some of my other colleagues. But there is no necessity that we should be in agreement. In a country of this kind there are many questions upon which the patriotic duty is to agree or disagree, to respect each one's liberty, to entertain the opinions he entertains, and, so long as he is within the law, and to act upon those opinions. As I have pointed out, no substantial difference of opinion is involved here. But it is not conducive to any good purpose to endeavour to bring about an agreement concerning certain matters when we all know that we shall not succeed in the effort. . Let us learn, after all, to respect our respective opinions, to respect the liberties of each man to form his own opinions upon such questions as are involved here, to respect the right of each man to act conscientiously upon his own opinion within the law, and we shall get along a great deal better. I trust that the hon. member for Quebec East may have performed this valuable service: that he has caused it to be made perfectly clear that in the action that was taken there was no refusal to recognize the status of any organization because of the religious belief of its members. That is a good thing to have made clear. As regards the particular action that took place, and as regards the particular conference, I think it is equally clear that there is no room for criticism. And for the rest, may we not hope that after this debate we shall realize perhaps more fully than we did before the wisdom of recognizing the liberty of opinion to which I have referred and the liberty of action within the law upon the conscientious opinions which each one may hold.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I hope the Minister of Labour will accept that doctrine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with all due deference and respect to the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), I must say that notwithstanding his explanation, I am no clearer upon this subject than I was at six o'clock. Having listened intently to the able speech of the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) I had come to the conclusion that a labour congress or conference was to be held in Canada under the auspices of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) in the month of May next, and that it was to be a general and universal labour congress or conference. If that is the case, the point made by the member for Quebec East is unassailable-that is, that all labour unions in Canada should have been invited to participate in that conference. Now comes the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government with the statement that the labour conference is going to be held as between employers and employees in one particular trade, the building trade. If that is true, I do not see the necessity of inviting the unions referred to this afternoon, though, as has been admitted by the Prime Minister himself, a large number of persons engaged in the building trades are members of the national so-called Catholic unions. Even if only one thousand out of the thirty-nine thousand members of the National Labour Union were connected with the building trades, they should be represented at that conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me, I think he has not fully grasped the statement of the Prime Minister. It was that this was to be a conference between a certain association of employers in the building trades and certain associations of workmen in the building trades, certain distinct bodies, not a general conference even of the entire building trades of the Dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Railways and Canals,-salaries, contingencies, $230,025.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
May I suggest to the
minister that, in view of the notice given by the Prime Minister as to an inquiry into railway matters in another form, it would be wise for my hon. friend to defer for a day or two these Estimates? I do not want to press the matter unduly; but in view of the general discussion likely to be raised on that motion, we may be duplicating our work by going into railway matters to-night. I quite realize, of course, that it was mentioned yesterday evening that Railway Estimates would be taken up to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister
intended going on with Labour Estimates this evening, but unfortunately it is impossible for him to be present. I could take up Civil Government and a few other items to which there could not be much objection. Some members want to get information in connection with the Railway Estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: With the promise of an early adjournment, the minister might, perhaps, make some progress.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: What salaries are generally paid to agents at various stations on the line?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Before this question
is answered and before any other questions of a like nature are asked, I think it only fair, in order that nobody may be called to order, to point out that when we reach the item providing the large amount for the administration of the Canadian National Railways, these questions and all other questions concerning the administration of the Canadian National Railways will be perfectly in order and may be asked, and there will be no desire whatever on the part of the Chair to restrict any such questions. As regards the outside service or the administration of the lines by a commission, the Chair must now rule that questions concerning these are not in order upon an item providing for Civil Government, which is merely the payment of employees in the department at Ottawa.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: With reference to civil government, during the last fiscal year we had 104 employees and the salaries paid totalled $208,204.91. During the coming fiscal year our staff will be reduced to 95, and the total amount that we ask for is $201,425.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
What offices have been
abolished?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: On page 96 of the Estimates the details in regard to every officer in the department are shown. The hon. member will see, by the details, the offices that have been abolished, because they are not included in the 1921-22 list.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Who decided to abolish
all these offices?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: There are some positions that we have abolished on the recommendation of the deputy minister, which recommendation is approved by the Civil Service Commission. We had a staff under Mr. Monsarrat that were not further required when the Quebec bridge was completed, and we took them over and used them in connection with the railways. We have abolished four or five positions there. On page 96 the hon. member will see the title "Head statistical clerk." Some employees in the Statistical branch were taken over by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
If Mr. Monsarrat was
on the Quebec bridge, would he not belong to the Outside Service?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Yes. We brought him here, and he was here in the department after the Quebec bridge was completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I understand that these changes in the staff were decided upon the recommendation of the deputy minister as approved by the Civil Service Commission?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: That is, the Civil Service Commission is the body which decides whether the staff shall be increased or decreased, and not the minister or the deputy minister?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The deputy recommends the decrease of the staff or the abolition of an office, and the Civil Service Commission must approve.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
That is as regards the
Inside Service. The Outside Service is also under the control of the Civil Service Commission?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
In exactly the same
way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And it is the duty of the management of the railways to look after the employees on the railways?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: When the Civil Service Act was passed by Parliament, railways were excepted in so far as the Civil Service Commission was concerned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: If the minister has no control over the Inside Service of his department, no control over the Outside Service and no control over the employees of the different railways, why have we a minister at all?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: What are the duties of the minister?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
In view of the very large portion of the hon. gentleman's department which has been transferred to the Board of Directors at Toronto, there must be much less work to be
9 p.m. done in his department than formerly. This year and last year the reduction in the staff has not been very great, but there may have been in previous years a reduction to correspond with the decrease in the work. Has there been any decrease in the staff at Ottawa, having in view the large part of the business now transferred to Toronto?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I cannot say that there has been much reduction. Prior to the Government railways passing to the management of the Canadian National Railway system, the details of the work in connection with the Government railways were largely done at Moncton, so that the work was merely transferred from Moncton to the Canadian National railway management, and the work has not decreased as regards the Railway Department. On account of the system being enlarged by the taking over of the Canadian Northern, there is more correspondence and more work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I see that last year
there were four senior clerk-stenographers, and that this year there are ten. On the other hand, there were fourteen clerk-stenographers last year, as compared with eight this year. By what process have so many clerk-stenographers become senior clerk-stenographers with an increase in salary?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The increase is due to the reclassification by the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I thuoght the reclassification was to reduce the salaries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: It increased the salaries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
What are the duties of
the hydraulic engineer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
He has to do all the
engineering work in connection with the canals, the Welland and St. Lawrance canals, for instance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
He has to do with water-powers ?
- Hon. Mr. REID:	Yes, and work generally in connection with the canals.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Has he anything to do
with providing water for the locomotives and things of that sort?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Would the minister explain why the chief engineer's salary has been raised from $6,000 to $8,000?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: That is a typographical error, and I intend to move to reduce that by $2,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I notice that there
are three secretaries to executives. What are the functions of these gentlemen, and who are the executives in the Railway Department?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
The deputy minister
has a secretary, and so has the chief engineer, and the comptroller. These positions were classified by the Civil Service Commission in that way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
I see we are asked to
vote the salary of a solicitor and counsel, and further down in the list I see "assistant solicitor." I am very much surprised that the department should have these officials, because I understood we had taken over the legal staff of no less than three railroads. I understand these staffs are still at work and, extraordinary to relate, some of them are fighting the Government, but nevertheless we are supposed to pay the cost. If we have all these legal gentlemen why should we retain a counsel in the department, or if the departmental counsel is a competent man, as I trust he is, why not dismiss the others? The time has come for strict economy. In former years my hon. friend the minister would come to Parliament, and, with his very pleasant ways, get his Estimates through without much difficulty, but this year I think even his genial smile will not allow him to get his Estimates through so easily in view of the serious railway situation confronting this country.
Furthermore, I do not think it is reasonable for the minister to try and screen himself behind the Civil Service Commission. Whenever any information is asked as to the salaries of any of these officials, the minister says: That was done by the Civil Service Commission. Now the minister is either responsible or irresponsible. If he is responsible, he is the man who should give us the information. If he is not responsible, he should not be there at all. I should like him to give us a full explanation concerning the legal staff of his department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: We have in the department a solicitor and an assistant solicitor. Their time is occupied very largely in drawing up leases and contracts, and doing other work of that kind. There is a large amount of that work to be done in the department. Very important cases that have to go to court are referred to the Justice Department, after a brief has been prepared in our department. These important cases that go to court are not in charge of our own counsel. We have always had a solicitor in the department for the departmental work, and I can assure my hon. friend that there is sufficient to keep him busy all the time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: These men in the department are drawing up leases?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
And agreements and
contracts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I do not think the minister can seriously contend that a man with the title of head counsel for the department, and the assistant counsel, are occupied simply in drawing up leases. I know something about legal work and about leases. We do not need a head counsel to draw up leases because it is simply routine work. The minister mentioned a moment ago that most of the legal work of his department was referred to the Justice Department, and was done, apparently, by the officials of that department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Oh, no. I say that some
cases are referred to the Department of Justice, which is the legal department for all the other departments of the Government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Then why refer these
cases to the Department of Justice if they are handled by the Department of Railways and Canals?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The brief is prepared by the solictor for our department, who understands the matter, but if it is a very important case it may be referred to the Justice Department, who will pass on it finally. If you have a legal gentleman doing that work, he is entitled to the title of solicitor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: This gentleman does not do any work in court?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
He is there to assist
the counsel that acts for the Government. He would prepare the brief.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Where cases go before
the court, the Justice Department selects the counsel?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
But our department
counsel prepare the whole case, as well as assist the outside counsel in court. A number of cases arise from time to time that must go before the court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Then if the department
solicitor does all that preparatory work, why does he not go to court and save the expense of engaging another man?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows that the counsel employed in cases that go before the Exchequer Court or the Supreme Court is usually a gentleman who has had experience in these courts. Generally these men command a large fee. The salary paid to our solicitor is $5,000. You would not expect a man drawing that
salary to have the same experience as a counsel handling very important cases involving a large amount of money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
If, according to the
statement of the minister, the departmental counsel is not competent to appear in court-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
He does appear in
court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: But the minister said a moment ago that we had to retain outside counsel because his own counsel had not enough experience and was not competent to appear in court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: What I said was that he appears as solicitor assisting the senior counsel in court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I quite realize that no large business enterprise can be properly carried on without the assistance of lawyers. That is a self-evident proposition. But what I want to be clear upon is this: Does the Railway Board now operate the Intercolonial?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: That being so, why should we have counsel engaged in railway matters in Ottawa and also a large staff of counsel in Toronto?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And in Montreal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And in Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And in Moncton.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
Yes, in Montreal,
Quebec, and Moncton.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And Toronto. .

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I said Toronto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And Brome.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
No, not in Brome.
The people in Brome are so honest and fair and sensible that we do not have lawsuits with the railways. I want to know why it is that we should have a large staff in Toronto when there are counsel in Ottawa.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: There are many cases in connection with the Intercolonial that are yet to come before the courts; and it is only a short time ago since the Canadian Northern was taken over. Probably in the near future however, we shall be able to reduce the staff. There are a number of cases in connection with the Intercolonial on which the solicitor is busy all the time getting ready his briefs. Those cases are about to go to the Exchequer Court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
The minister says
that lawyers are preparing leases. Are not the right of way agent and the assistant right of way agent competent to do this work?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: They are not solicitors. We have a right of way lease agent who is employed to value properties, but he has nothing to do with drawing leases.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the principal work of the departmental counsel is the drawing up of such agreements.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
That is one of his
duties.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: The minister said it was his main work. My own experience as a lawyer in my constituency and around Quebec is different. Whenever the Transcontinental railway expropriates land in the county of Dorchester, or in neighbouring constituencies through which it passes; the agreements and leases are not drawn up by departmental counsel, but by friends of the Government. I want to call the attention of the minister to the fact that some of the gentlemen who do this work are most dilatory. I do not know whether they get paid on the basis of the time they take to do the work of the department, but I know that, in certain cases of expropriation in my constituency, farmers who entered into agreements had to wait for months before they could get their money from the department. I do not think the minister can fairly make the statement that leases and agreements are drawn up by this gentleman to whom we pay $5,000 when I know, as a matter of fact, that in the city of Quebec friends of the Government are engaged to do the work. I am not blaming the Government for throwing work in the way of their friends; but whenever I have advised any of my people in Dorchester, or any people in Quebec, to enter into agreements, I have observed that the department has never made the mistake of sending them to a Liberal notary. They always happen to strike a good Tory. Now, why should we go to the expense of getting outside help when we pay this gentleman for drawing up leases? Are the leases drawn up in Ottawa, and sent to these Tory notaries in Quebec-and I suppose it is the same all over the province-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: All over.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
-are they drawn up in Ottawa and sent to these men merely for

the sake of giving them a little money? The hon. minister cannot afford to bestow these gifts on his friends. His department ought to be run strictly on economical principles, and if we are paying $5,000 to someone to draw leases he ought to do the work. The Government, I submit, should change the present system and save money; but if they do happen to take outside legal help, as they have done of late, the minister ought to see to it that whoever does the work does it expeditiously and with satisfaction to those concerned. At present there is no satisfaction. For example, there was an expropriation in my constituency at St. Malachie, where a sand pit was taken over by the Transcontinental. Representatives of the Government went there and made a certain agreement, and a notary from the neighbouring parish who belongs to my hon. friend's constituency of Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier), a Mr. McKenzie, was engaged. This man has kept the parties waiting months and months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Is he a census commissioner?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: Evidently the Government was so well satisfied with his work in this connection that they have appointed him census enumerator in the same constituency. He is one of the strongest Tories, and while I do not blame the Government for giving their friends some work, I think they should have the courage to get up in the House and admit it. This gentleman received the documents for examination and study and although they were in his hands for months he kept the farmers waiting for quite a while. Now, such a condition of things should be remedied, and if Tory notaries do not give satisfaction, then the minister should try others, even though they may be Liberals, provided that they do the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: As they will.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext: And as Liberals always do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MINISTER OF LABOUR AND THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC LABOUR UNIONS
speechtext:
